name: Shengling Shi
department: Delft Center for Systems and Control
intro: I work at the intersection of artificial intelligence, system identification, and optimal control, with applications to biological and bio-inspired systems.
research_intro: Our group develops methods and theory for learning dynamical systems and controlling them safely and efficiently. We study human motion digital twins, assistive robotics, and biological networks.
bio: I am an Assistant Professor at the Delft Center for Systems and Control, TU Delft. Before joining the faculty, I was a postdoctoral associate at MIT and a postdoctoral researcher at TU Delft. I received my PhD in 2021, advised by Prof. Paul M. J. van den Hof, and my MSc with distinction in 2017, both from the Control Systems Group at Eindhoven University of Technology. During my master's studies, I completed a research internship at ETH Zurich. I obtained my bachelor's degree from Harbin Institute of Technology.
service: I have served as an associate editor for the IFAC World Congress and am a member of the IFAC Technical Committee on Modelling, Identification and Signal Processing.

research.title: Learning-based optimal control
research.short: Performance and safety guarantees for control with learned or uncertain models.
research.description: How can we control large-scale or partially unknown systems while retaining rigorous guarantees? We develop and analyze model predictive control, approximate dynamic programming, and control barrier functions, with a focus on performance, safety, and computational efficiency.
research.alt: A control-theoretic surface and its level set, from the group's research
research.caption: Performance analysis and safety constraints in learning-based control.

research.title: AI for bio-inspired systems
research.short: Human motion digital twins, musculoskeletal systems, and tendon-driven robots.
research.description: We bring learning and optimal control to nonlinear, high-dimensional systems, particularly human musculoskeletal models and tendon-driven assistive robots. Our work explores reinforcement learning, generative models, and efficient numerical methods for applications in healthcare and human movement.
research.alt: A simulated human musculoskeletal model with leg muscles shown in red
research.caption: A musculoskeletal model for studying human motion and control.

research.title: Learning dynamical networks
research.short: Data-driven modeling and identification of interconnected dynamical systems.
research.description: Complex systems consist of interacting subsystems. We study how network structure and dynamics can be identified from limited measurements and excitation signals, with applications including effective connectivity in brain networks.
research.alt: Brain imaging slices highlighting regions used in network analysis
research.caption: Brain imaging provides an application for learning dynamical networks.

news.text: Two bachelor research groups successfully defended their thesis projects on robotic-hand control and human motion digital twins.
We presented preliminary results on human motion digital twins at the Benelux Meeting on Systems and Control.
DCSC launched a monthly online seminar series. The spring speakers were Leilei Cui, Sungho Shin, Dinesh Krishnamoorthy, and Lars Lindemann.
Congratulations to Kanghui He on successfully defending his PhD thesis on safe and computationally efficient learning-based control!
Changrui Liu's work on the regret of MPC with imperfect inputs was featured at CDC 2025 in Brazil.
Our paper on state-action control barrier functions appeared online in IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control.
Shengling attended IROS 2025 in Hangzhou, China.
Our preprint on bang-ride optimal control and fast battery charging is available on arXiv.
Our paper on the suboptimality of receding horizon quadratic control appeared online in IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control.
Kelvin Toonen joined the group as a PhD student, working on learning and control for human digital twins.
Shengling joined TU Delft as an Assistant Professor.
Shengling joined MIT as a postdoctoral associate, working on optimal control for large-scale nonlinear systems.
